The majority voted in favour of [adjourning the debate](http://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2017-09-11.217.1) and so put off further discussion on these bills until a later time. ### What do the bills do? The two bills are the: * [Broadcasting Legislation Amendment (Broadcasting Reform) Bill 2017](http://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/r5907); and the * [Commercial Broadcasting (Tax) Bill 2017](http://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/r5908). Most significantly, the bills were introduced to get rid of certain media ownership, control and diversity laws, like the ‘75% audience reach rule’, which stops commercial television broadcasting licensees from controlling licences if the combined licence area has a population over 75% of Australia' population. It would also get rid of the ‘2 out of 3 cross-media control rule’, which stops a company from having control over more than two out of three regulated media platforms in any one commercial radio licence area. Read more in the [bills digest](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd1718a/18bd08).

The Australian government introduced the Broadcasting Legislation Amendment (Broadcasting Reform) Bill 2017 to modernise media regulation, including repealing broadcasting licence fees and datacasting charges, abolishing the 75% audience reach rule and the two-out-of-three cross-media control rule, and extending anti-siphoning reforms, with a $4.6 million annual transitional support package for 19 broadcasters. The bill also increases local content obligations for regional television licensees following a trigger event and is part of a broader reform package announced on 6 May 2017, supported unanimously by the media industry.

The Commercial Broadcasting (Tax) Bill 2017 introduces a new spectrum tax to replace broadcasting licence fees, raising about $40 million annually and providing overall fee relief for broadcasters, with regional broadcasters paying significantly less based on transmitter power and spectrum use. The bill is part of the government's Broadcast and Content Reform Package, has unanimous industry support, and is contingent on the passage of the Broadcasting Reform Bill.

Labor supported the majority of the broadcasting reform bills but opposed repealing the two-out-of-three cross-media rule, warning it would worsen Australia’s already high media ownership concentration and harm diversity, and criticised the government’s piecemeal approach for lacking holistic, evidence-based reform.

The speaker argued for the Broadcasting Legislation Amendment (Broadcasting Reform) Bill 2017, which abolishes the 75 per cent reach rule and the two-out-of-three cross-media rule, introduces higher local content obligations for regional commercial television licensees after ownership changes, and abolishes broadcasting licence fees while maintaining other diversity rules and the anti-siphoning list for major sporting events.

The speaker argued against repealing the two-out-of-three rule, which limits media owners to two of three platforms (radio, TV, newspaper) in a market, citing that Murdoch-owned titles account for 64.2% of metropolitan circulation and Fairfax 26.4%, and that further concentration would harm democratic diversity. They supported other measures in the bill, including licence fee relief, but opposed removing the ownership restriction.

The speaker argued that the Broadcasting Legislation Amendment (Broadcasting Reform) Bill 2017 is necessary to modernise Australian media law, citing the 90% decline in Prime Media's value over a decade and a 14% drop in newspaper advertising in 2016, and supported abolishing the two-out-of-three and 75% ownership rules, reducing broadcast licence fees, banning gambling ads during children's sports broadcasts, revising the antisiphoning list, and providing a $30 million package for women's and niche sports on subscription TV.

The government argued that the Broadcasting Legislation Amendment Bill 2017 and Commercial Broadcasting (Tax) Bill 2017 will abolish broadcasting licence fees, introduce a spectrum tax, and remove the 75% audience reach rule and two-out-of-three rule while maintaining protections for local content and competition, with the package having unanimous media industry support.
The Commercial Broadcasting (Tax) Bill 2017 supports the Broadcasting Legislation Amendment (Broadcasting Reform) Bill 2017, particularly regarding spectrum fees, and was commended to the House.

Labor will not oppose the two amendments to the Broadcasting Legislation Amendment (Broadcasting Reform) Bill 2017 concerning programming requirements and trigger events, but argued the government’s media reform deal was made behind closed doors, citing 61% voter disapproval, $30 million in taxpayer-funded handouts to Fox Sports, and unanswered questions about a journalism innovation fund.

The speaker argued that the Broadcasting Legislation Amendment Bill 2017 is opposed by 61% of Australians and will cause job losses in regional Australia, not job creation. They criticised government deals with crossbenchers, including a $60 million fund for the Nick Xenophon Team and a competitive neutrality inquiry targeting the ABC.

The speaker argued that the Broadcasting Legislation Amendment (Broadcasting Reform) Bill 2017 is urgently needed to help Australian media businesses compete with global internet companies, and criticised the shadow minister for opposing the reforms with illogical arguments, including a claim that industry support for the bill disqualified it.
